---
title: "Open Science"
---

The term "Open science" is a wide term, that has been used and interpreted in different ways. There are also a number of competing terms, such as "Open Research" or "Science 2.0". A good way to start to understand what open science is and isn't is to look at the UNESCO Recommendation on Open Science @unescounescorecommendationopen2021. The Recommendation takes a broad view of science, giving a definition that includes all different fields of scholarly activities not just the hard sciences. The definition given for open science reads as follows:

> For the purpose of this Recommendation, open science is defined as an inclusive construct that combines various movements and practices aiming to make multilingual scientific knowledge openly available, accessible and reusable for everyone, to increase scientific collaborations and sharing of information for the benefits of science and society, and to open the processes of scientific knowledge creation, evaluation and communication to societal actors beyond the traditional scientific community. It comprises all scientific disciplines and aspects of scholarly practices, including basic and applied sciences, natural and social sciences and the humanities, and it builds on the following key pillars: open scientific knowledge, open science infrastructures, science communication, open engagement of societal actors and open dialogue with other knowledge systems.
[@unescounescorecommendationopen2021, p 7]

![Different pieces of the puzzle comprising open science according to UNESCO](../img/unesco-open-science.png)

Sweden was among the UNESCO members that approved the recommendation. In the Swedish context, the National Library of Sweden has developed national guidelines for open science @nationallibraryofswedennationalguidelinesopen2024 where six different areas of focus are mentioned. Those are:

> - Open access to scholarly publications  
- Open access to research data  
-  Open research methods  
- Open educational resources  
- Public engagement in science  
- Infrastructures supporting open science
   [@nationallibraryofswedennationalguidelinesopen2024, p 8]

These areas do not cover the full breadth of the UNESCO recommendation, and neither will this course. However, we will cover most of the areas defined by the National library, and also some more. 
The impact of open science may also differ between different research areas - let´s start with listening to Thomas Crouzier, a KTH researcher who shares his experiences of different aspects of open science practices. First, Thomas tells us about his research and how he became engaged in open science and discovered useful digital tools.

Thomas did a report on the impact of a transition towards Open Science on the stakeholders in the research ecosystem for the European commission @europeancommission.directorategeneralforresearchandinnovation.scienceecosystem202015. An important part of open science is open access to scientific publications.
